transcript.text:
That's annoying! Here are the most common causes, roughly in order of how often they're the culprit:

If it won't turn on at all:
1. Check the socket. Plug something else in to make sure it's working.
2. Check the plug fuse. UK plugs have a fuse inside (usually 13A for vacuums). Swap it with a known-good one if you have a spare.
3. Inspect the cable. Look for cuts, kinks or scorch marks. Don't use it if the cable's damaged.
4. Let it cool down. Many vacuums have a thermal cut-out that switches them off if they overheat (often due to a blockage). Unplug it and leave it for 30–60 minutes, then try again.
5. If it's cordless, make sure the battery is charged and properly clicked in. Check whether the charger light comes on.

If it runs but has poor or no suction:
1. Empty the bin or change the bag. Even a half-full bag can kill suction.
2. Clean or replace the filters. Clogged filters are a huge cause of weak suction (and overheating). Many can be rinsed, but let them dry fully (24 hours) before refitting.
3. Check for blockages. Look in the hose, wand and where the hose connects to the body. A broom handle can push things through the hose.
4. Check the brush bar. Hair and thread wrap around it and can stop it spinning. Snip it free with scissors.
5. Check the belt (on upright models). If the brush bar doesn't spin, the belt may have snapped or slipped.

When to stop:
If it smells of burning, sparks, or still won't work after the above, it's likely the motor or an internal electrical fault. That's best left to a repair shop or the manufacturer, especially if it's still under warranty.

What make and model is it, and what exactly is it doing (or not doing)? I can give more specific steps.
its a Henry, the red one with the smiley face. it just stopped while i was doing the stairs and wont come back on. the lamp works in the socket

Henrys are tough and very fixable, so there's a good chance this is something simple. Stopping suddenly on the stairs points to a few likely causes:

1. The plug fuse (most likely first check)
On stairs the cable often gets tugged, and a sudden stop is classic blown-fuse behaviour. Unscrew the plug and swap the fuse for a 13A one from another appliance you know works. If Henry springs back to life, buy a replacement fuse.

2. Overheating
If the bag was full or the hose partly blocked, the motor can overheat and cut out. Unplug him, leave him for an hour, then:
• Check the bag (they fill up faster than you'd think)
• Check the hose for blockages, especially at both ends
• Check the round filter under the head

3. Cable damage
Being dragged up and down stairs is hard on the cable. Unwind it fully and look along its length, especially near the plug and where it goes into Henry's head. Look for kinks, cuts, or exposed wires. If you find damage, don't use it.

4. Worn motor brushes
If he's a few years old and none of the above helps, the motor's carbon brushes may have worn out. This often makes the motor stop suddenly, sometimes after a bit of sparking or a burning smell. It's a common, cheap repair. Brushes or a replacement motor are easy to get, and many vacuum repair shops fix Henrys routinely.

5. The switch
Less common, but the on/off switch on top can fail. Also a repair-shop job, and inexpensive.

Start with the fuse, since it takes two minutes. If that doesn't do it, let me know how old he is and whether you noticed any smell or noise before he stopped.
I haven't got a screwdriver or a spare fuse. There's black tape on the wire near the plug, my son did it ages ago, and it's a bit bent there. No smell or bang that I noticed.

That taped, bent bit near the plug is very likely the culprit. Cables often break internally right next to the plug, where they flex most, and stairs are exactly where it gets tugged. A wire inside can snap or come loose even when the outside looks fine.

Please don't use Henry for now. Insulating tape isn't a safe long-term fix for mains cable. If the wires inside are damaged, there's a risk of shock or the cable overheating. Even if wiggling it brings him back to life, it'll keep happening and could get worse.

The good news is it's an easy, cheap fix:

• Shorten the cable and fit a new plug. Since the damage is right by the plug, the usual repair is to cut the cable off a few inches past the taped section and wire on a new 13A plug. You'd lose a little length, but Henry's cable is long. A new plug costs a few pounds and comes with a fuse.
• Replace the whole cable. Numatic (Henry's maker) sells replacement cables if you'd rather keep the full length, but fitting one means opening Henry's head, so it's more involved.

Who can do it:
• A local vacuum or appliance repair shop will do this quickly and cheaply, often while you wait. They see Henrys all the time.
• Anyone handy with a screwdriver, perhaps your son again, could fit a new plug. Just make sure it's done properly this time rather than taped.

If the plug and cable are sorted and he still won't start, the next suspects would be the fuse (a new plug would rule that out anyway) or the motor brushes. But I'd bet on the cable.
